To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the human visual system exhibits hysteresis during dynamic transitions between objects and scenes.

the dynamic transition between scene and object perception exhibits a hysteresis phenomenon that is not purely decisional, is more prominent for transitions from object to scene than from scene to object, is not affected by the task, and resists changes in the movie stimulus.
observers perceive scenes and objects in dynamic image sequences for longer if they started at a scene view and object view, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms underlying dynamic scene and object perception.
the perception of dynamic scenes and objects, and the hysteresis in this dynamic perception.
understanding the dynamic nature of the visual system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this paper provides evidence for hysteresis in dynamic scene perception, which is consistent with a dynamic balance between object and scene processing.
the hysteresis phenomenon is an important and interesting aspect of the visual system and that it is likely to be a useful tool in understanding visual processing.
the current study provides evidence that the human visual system exhibits a strong tendency to perceive scenes and objects as a function of their perceptual history.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the visual system can be biased toward either scene or object processing, and the bias is determined by the prior perception.
the human visual system is biased toward the processing of scenes over objects, but this bias is modulated by the perceptual history of the observer.
the human visual system has a tendency to maintain a perceptual history, which may be useful in the perception of naturalistic visual scenes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the visual system may not be a passive observer of the visual world, but rather an active participant in the construction and interpretation of visual scenes.
the human visual system has a strong tendency to perceive a scene as a scene and an object as an object, even when the stimulus is not clearly a scene or an object.
perception is influenced by prior perceptual experience.
